title: Introduction to Graphs
prerequisites: Comfort with reading bar graphs and histograms from Chapter 5.
Basic idea of ordered pairs and coordinates from earlier classes.
Understanding of direct proportion from Chapter 13 (for linear graphs).

topics.title: The Coordinate Plane & Plotting Points
topics.quick_summary: The Cartesian coordinate plane uses two perpendicular number lines (the x-axis and y-axis) to uniquely locate any point using an ordered pair (x, y).

detailed.definition: The coordinate plane is formed by a horizontal x-axis and a vertical y-axis intersecting at the origin (0,0); any point is located by its ordered pair (x, y), where x is the horizontal distance and y is the vertical distance from the origin.
detailed.key_idea: The ORDER in the ordered pair (x, y) matters — the x-coordinate (abscissa) is always written and read first, followed by the y-coordinate (ordinate); (2,3) and (3,2) represent two completely different points.
detailed.working_principle: To plot (x, y): starting at the origin, move x units horizontally (right if positive, left if negative), then move y units vertically (up if positive, down if negative) from that position, and mark the resulting point.
applications: Mapping and navigation systems, computer graphics, and data visualization all rely on coordinate plotting.
Representing relationships between two variables (like time and distance, or price and demand) visually as graphs.

topics.real_life: GPS coordinates (latitude, longitude) and pixel positions on a computer screen both use the same idea as the Cartesian coordinate plane to pinpoint an exact location.
points: Every point is written as an ordered pair (x, y): x = abscissa (horizontal), y = ordinate (vertical).
The origin is the point (0, 0), where both axes intersect.
The plane is divided into 4 quadrants by the two axes, numbered counter-clockwise starting from the top-right (Quadrant I: x>0,y>0).
Points on the x-axis always have y = 0; points on the y-axis always have x = 0.
mistakes: Swapping the order of x and y coordinates while plotting a point.
Plotting a point in the wrong quadrant due to a sign error on either coordinate.
Forgetting that a point lying exactly ON an axis has one coordinate equal to zero.
topics.memory_hook: 'x before y, always' — 'Along the corridor (x), then up the stairs (y)' is a classic way to remember plotting order.
topics.advanced: The coordinate plane, formalized by René Descartes, is the reason algebra and geometry could be unified into a single subject — every algebraic equation in x and y can now be 'seen' as a geometric graph, and every geometric shape can be described using algebraic equations, a connection exploited constantly through the rest of mathematics.

topics.title: Linear Graphs & Reading Graphs (Bar, Line, and Time-Distance)
topics.quick_summary: A linear graph is a straight-line graph representing a relationship where one quantity changes at a constant rate with respect to another, commonly used for tracking quantities like distance, temperature, or cost over time.

detailed.definition: A linear graph is the graph of a linear relationship (such as y = kx or y = mx + c), always appearing as a straight line on the coordinate plane; reading a graph means extracting specific values or trends by interpreting the plotted line or points.
detailed.key_idea: On a linear graph, the STEEPNESS (slope) of the line reflects the rate of change of one quantity with respect to the other — a steeper line means a faster rate of change (e.g., higher speed on a distance-time graph).
detailed.working_principle: To read a value from a graph, locate the known coordinate on one axis, trace perpendicular to the line/curve until you reach it, then trace across to read the corresponding value on the other axis; to plot a linear relationship, calculate a few (x,y) pairs from the equation and connect them with a straight line.
applications: Distance-time graphs used in physics to represent constant or changing speed.
Tracking trends over time such as temperature variation, population growth, or savings growth in finance.

topics.real_life: A car travelling at constant speed produces a straight-line distance-time graph, while a fixed hourly wage produces a straight-line earnings-vs-hours graph.
points: A straight-line graph always represents a relationship where equal changes in x produce equal changes in y (constant rate).
If a linear graph passes through the origin, the two quantities are in direct proportion (y = kx).
On a distance-time graph, a horizontal line segment (zero slope) represents the object being at rest (not moving).
A steeper line on a distance-time graph always represents a faster/higher speed than a less steep line.
mistakes: Misreading a value off the graph by tracing along the wrong axis or losing track of the scale of each axis.
Assuming EVERY straight line graph must pass through the origin — only DIRECT proportion graphs do; general linear graphs (y = mx + c with c ≠ 0) do not.
Confusing a horizontal graph segment (object at rest) with a graph that has zero steepness meaning zero value — they are different ideas.
topics.memory_hook: 'Steeper line, faster change' — the slope of a linear graph always tells the story of the rate of change.
topics.advanced: Distance-time graphs are a student's first real encounter with the idea of 'slope equals rate' that becomes central to calculus in later years — the intuitive idea that a steeper line means faster change smoothly generalizes into the formal concept of a derivative, making this simple graph-reading skill a genuine mathematical foundation stone.
